description: The agreement half of the adjacency ruling, for the containers where both spellings are malformed and so cannot be proven as a value, plus the round-2 review finding on the entry lookahead and the regression the ruling's direction had to avoid. A newline separates exactly like a space (`spec/grammar.md:248`), so the newline and spaced spellings of the parenthesized source must produce the SAME diagnostics -- the assertion is that they are malformed in the SAME WAY, not merely that they are malformed. Its execution twin, `core-language/expressions/a-newline-separates-like-a-space`, runs the same shapes in the container where both spellings are well-formed. Neither fixture could have detected the ADJACENCY ruling specifically: the container that exhibited it differed only in its AST, and a fixture sees events and diagnostics, never a tree. THIS fixture is load-bearing all the same, and the scoping matters -- do not read 'not an adjacency witness' as 'proves nothing' and prune it. It is the core-language witness for the OTHER mechanism in this slice, the phantom unmatched-delimiter report: measured whole-file at `0277d5ff` it raised 11 diagnostics (`ol-unmatched-paren` x4, `ol-missing-end` x3, `ol-bad-token` x4), and here it raises 19, with the parenthesized rows raising the substituted `ol-bad-token` and no `ol-unmatched-paren` at all. Its twin, by contrast, passes unchanged against that same pre-fix parser. The comprehension and control rows are the guard: a newline after a header selects the long `... end` body form (`spec/grammar.md:34`), so the `[` binds as a BODY rather than as a selector on the header's last operand, and each raises `ol-missing-end`. A narrowing can only make the `[` LESS likely to bind, so those are strictly more protected than before -- asserted here rather than assumed, and asserted in their SPLIT form, which is the only form that exercises the newline. The dict rows pin `spec/grammar.md:314`: a call still owed an operand is unfinished exactly as an operator is, so the unfinished value's own grammar position wins and no entry opens. Measured at `0277d5ff` before the fix -- and stated for the SPLIT spelling, because an earlier version of this description attributed it to the one-line spelling, which is false -- `{ a: sentence 1` + newline + `mod: 2 }` parsed CLEAN into two entries, `a` and `mod`, leaving `sentence` one argument short, which `check()` then reported as `ol-not-enough-inputs` on a program the grammar says is simply a malformed entry -- as its own `{ a: 1 + b: 2 }` example is. The one-line `{ a: sentence 1 mod: 2 }` behaved correctly at that tip: it raised `ol-bad-token` twice at parse stage, opened no entry keyed `mod`, and so never reached `check()` at all. The newline was the whole of the difference, which is this slice's thesis. Both spellings of each are here because the one-line and multi-line forms must agree; the complete-call counterpart, where the key DOES open its entry, pulls the opposite way and is pinned in `packages/parser/src/newline-continuations-and-delimiters.test.mjs`. On `message`: this fixture deliberately does NOT set `compareMessages` (issue #1025 review round 2). Its `ol-bad-token` prose is `i don't know how to read <word> here.` plus the shared ownership clause, and only the CLAUSE is a cross-stage contract -- comparing the whole string would also freeze the prefix, which `spec/error-model.md:110` constrains in content but not in words and `:262-264` positively permits an implementation to reword. The property that matters here, that the parse stage reuses the SAME ownership sentence as `ol-reserved-word`, is pinned instead by `packages/parser/src/misplaced-keyword-message.test.mjs`, which reads the sibling code's EMITTED message and asserts this one ends with it -- agreement proved by derivation rather than by freezing English, and the only form of it another implementation could not be expected to share anyway.
